items.name: Balance you don't have to think about
items.why: Read this before the drills that follow it. The standing balance ladder makes balance harder by taking information away. These drills work the other way: they park your attention on a task — a stick, a ball, a count — so balance has to run underneath, without you steering it.

fields.release:
Most balance practice has you thinking about balancing. That builds the skill, but daily life almost never asks for it in that form — you catch yourself while carrying groceries, turning to answer someone, stepping off a kerb mid-thought. The system that saves you there is the one running when you are NOT paying attention to it.

So these drills give your attention a job somewhere else. Follow the stick. Catch the ball. Count backwards. The balance still has to happen for you to stay upright — and because you are not steering it, it learns to run on its own.
fields.notice: The difference between the first time and the tenth: early on, the task falls apart the moment balance gets loud. Later, both keep going at once. That shift — not longer holds, not harder surfaces — is what this storey trains.
fields.careful: Fair warning, once: stacking a task on top of balance means more to drop when it goes wrong. Earn the middle of the standing balance ladder first — one-leg stance, steady — before parking your attention elsewhere, and keep something to catch yourself on within reach at every rung of every drill here.

levels.name: Read it
levels.note: Once. It applies to every drill in this group.

evidence.grade: established in motor-learning research; the framing here is the app's own
evidence.basis: A large motor-learning literature finds that aiming attention at an external target or task improves balance performance and retention compared with thinking about the body itself, and dual-task balance training — a motor or cognitive task layered on a balance task — is standard practice in fall-prevention and return-from-injury rehabilitation. The specific drills that follow are coaching constructions of that principle, and their cards say so.

items.name: Wedge stance with a moving stick
items.equipment: A pair of wedges or a slant board; a stick (a broom handle works); a counter within reach

fields.tool: Wedges under the forefoot so the heels hang free, and a stick held in both hands.
fields.release: Stand with your toes up on the wedges, heels off the ground, knees bent. Hold the stick out in front of you. Sweep it slowly out to one side and back to the front, then the other side, following it the whole way with your eyes and head. The balance work is in what your feet and hips do while your attention rides the stick.
fields.notice: Where the wobble shows up when your head turns — feet, ankles, or hips — and whether following the stick with eyes-and-head is harder in one direction. Early on the sweep gets small and cautious; it widening again over sessions is the progress.
fields.careful: Heels-free on a wedge is a real ankle demand. If your ankles are unstable, earn the flat-floor version first and keep the counter within reach throughout. Knees stay bent — soft, not locked back.
fields.load: Calf raises and single-leg hip work on the same days, same reasoning as the balance ladder: the skill needs something underneath it that can hold.

levels.name: Flat floor
levels.note: Feet flat, knees bent, same stick sweep with eyes-and-head tracking. Earn the pattern before the wedges.

levels.name: On the wedges
levels.note: Toes on the wedges, heels free, knees bent. Counter within reach. Small sweeps first.

levels.name: Wider and slower
levels.note: Bigger sweep, slower travel, further behind you before returning. Slower is harder here, not easier.

evidence.grade: exploratory — a coaching construction; the underlying external-focus principle is established
evidence.basis: The drill combines forefoot balance with visual tracking so attention sits on the stick rather than the balancing. The video it came from claims this trains the body to use its strength more efficiently; that claim is the video's own and travels here as provenance, not as a finding.

items.sourceNote: From a coaching video flagged during intake, 11 Sep 2026 — a claim with a face attached, authored here in the app's own words.

items.name: Ball off the wall
items.equipment: A ball that bounces predictably (a tennis or reaction ball later), a wall, clear floor

fields.tool: A ball and a wall. Start with a slow, predictable ball — the bounce being boring is the point at first.
fields.release:
Face the wall, throw the ball against it, catch the return, repeat. Your attention rides the throw and the catch; the balance has to happen underneath for any of it to work.

Difficulty here is a set of dials, not one ladder. The rungs below are the footing dial — the balance half of the drill. The ball gives you the rest, each with an easy end and a hard end:

**Trajectory** — lob it high and soft, or throw it down straighter so the return comes back quick.
**Distance** — stand back for a long, lazy flight, or step in close so there is no time to think.
**Balls** — one, then two, then three or more; people work up to juggling them off the wall.
**Hands** — throw and catch with the same hand, or alternate hands every throw.
**Attention**, the top dial — look past the wall and catch in your peripheral vision, or count backwards by threes out loud while you go.

Pick a footing rung, set the ball dials where the catch just barely stays clean, and turn one dial at a time. When you raise one, it often pays to ease another back.
fields.notice: Which fails first — the catch, or the stance — and on the one-leg rung, which leg. Early on a quick return costs you the balance; later the leg just absorbs it. The dial that costs you the most is the one with the most to give.
fields.careful: Clear floor, nothing behind you, and a ball you are willing to drop — chasing a bad bounce on one leg is how this goes wrong. One dial at a time is the safety mechanism, not just the method. Losing the count is fine and expected; it is the drill telling you where its edge is.
fields.load: Same base as the ladder: calf and single-leg hip strength on the same days.

levels.name: Two feet
levels.note: Learn the throw-catch rhythm with balance cheap, and meet the ball dials here first.

levels.name: One leg
levels.note: Swap legs halfway — expect the sides to differ, and note which is which.

levels.name: Unstable footing
levels.note: Wobble or dome board — two feet first, one foot later. Counter within reach, and ease the ball dials back when you step up.

levels.name: Moving footing
levels.note: Stepping side to side, or a slow drift toward and away from the wall, between throws. The floor stops being a constant.

evidence.grade: established as a training approach; the dials are a common coaching vocabulary, not a tested protocol
evidence.basis: Dual-task balance training — motor tasks like catching, then cognitive tasks like serial subtraction, layered onto balance work — is standard in fall-prevention and return-to-sport rehabilitation, and progressions along exactly these axes (trajectory, distance, ball count, hands, footing) are used up to elite sport. No single trial tested this card as written.
